މާލިއްޔަތު ކޮމިޓީ

މި ކޮމިޓީގެ މަސްއޫލިއްޔަތުތަކުގެ ތެރޭގައި، ދައުލަތުގެ އިދާރާތަކުން ކުރާ އެކިއެކި ޚަރަދަކީ ޤާނޫނު ހުއްދަކުރާ ގޮތުގެމަތިން އަދި މަޖިލީހުން ފާސްކޮށްފައިވާ ބަޖެޓާ އެއްގޮތްވާ ގޮތުގެމަތިން ކުރާ ޚަރަދުތަކެއްތޯ ބެލުމާއި، މަޖިލީހުން ފާސްކުރާ ފައިސާގެ ޢަދަދުތައް ހޭދަކުރެވިގެން ނުވަތަ ޚަރަދުކުރެވިގެންދަނީ އެކަންކަމަށްތޯ ބެލުން ހިމެނެއެވެ. އަދި ހުއްދަކޮށްފައިވާ މިންވަރަށްވުރެ އިތުރަށް ދައުލަތުގެ އިދާރާތަކުން ފައިސާ ޚަރަދުކޮށްފައިވާނަމަ، އެގޮތަށް ފައިސާ ޚަރަދުކުރަންޖެހުނު ސަބަބާއި ޙާލަތު ކޮމިޓީން ބެލުން ހިމެނެއެވެ. މިގޮތުން ދައުލަތުގެ މާލިއްޔަތާ ގުޅޭގޮތުން ކަންކަން ބެލުމުގައި، ދައުލަތުގެ އިދާރާތަކާއި، ދައުލަތުން ހިއްސާވާ ކުންފުނިތަކާއި ދައުލަތުގެ ވިޔަފާރި އިދާރާތަކާއި، ދައުލަތުގެ މިނިވަން އިދާރާތަކުގެ މާލީ ހިސާބުތައް ދިރާސާކުރުމާއި، އޮޑިޓަރ ޖެނެރަލްގެ އެކިއެކި ރިޕޯޓުތައް ދިރާސާކުރުމާއި އަޅަންޖެހޭ ފިޔަވަޅުތައް ފާހަގަކޮށް، ދައުލަތުގެ ކަމާބެހޭ އިދާރާތަކަށް އެންގުން ހިމެނެއެވެ. މީގެ އިތުރުން، ދައުލަތަށް ލޯނު ނެގުމާއި ދައުލަތުގެ ފަރާތުން ގެރެންޓީ ދިނުމުގައި މަޖިލީހުގެ ފަރާތުން އަދާކުރަންޖެހޭ ދައުރާ ގުޅިގެން ކުރަންޖެހޭ ކަންކަން ކުރުމާއި، މޯލްޑިވްސް މަނިޓަރީ އޮތޯރިޓީއާއި އޮޑިޓަރ ޖެނެރަލްގެ އޮފީހުން ކުރާ މަސައްކަތްތައް ބެލުމާއި، އަދި ރައްޔިތުންގެ މަޖިލީހުން ކަނޑައަޅަންޖެހޭ މުސާރަތައް ކަނޑައެޅުމުގައި އެހެން ކޮމިޓީތަކުގެ މަޝްވަރާ ހޯދުން ހިމެނެއެވެ.

1. ތަޢާރުފް

މި ރިޕޯޓަކީ، ޤާނޫނު ނަންބަރު 4/2007 (އޮޑިޓް ޤާނޫނު) ގެ 20 ވަނަ މާއްދާގެ (ހ) ގެ ދަށުން އޮޑިޓަރ ޖެނެރަލް ހުށަހަޅުއްވާފައިވާ، އޮޑިޓަރ ޖެނެރަލްގެ އޮފީހުގެ 2027 ވަނަ އަހަރުގެ ބަޖެޓު، އެ މާއްދާގެ (ށ) ގެ ދަށުން އެ އޮފީހުގެ ބަޖެޓު ދިރާސާކުރުމުގެ މަސައްކަތް ރައްޔިތުންގެ މަޖިލީހަށް މަތިކޮށްފައިވާތީ، އެ މައްސަލަ މި ކޮމިޓީން ދިރާސާކޮށް ހުށަހަޅާ ރިޕޯޓެވެ. މި ރިޕޯޓުގައި ހިމަނާފައިވާ ޖަދުވަލުތަކަކީ މި ރިޕޯޓުގެ ބައެކެވެ.

2. ކޮމިޓީން މައްސަލަ ދިރާސާކުރުމުގައި ރިޢާޔަތްކުރި ލިޔުންތައް

މި މައްސަލަ ދިރާސާކުރުމުގައި އަންނަނިވި ލިޔެކިޔުންތަކަށް ކޮމިޓީން ރިޢާޔަތްކޮށްފައިވާނެއެވެ.

2.1. އޮޑިޓަރ ޖެނެރަލްގެ އޮފީހުގެ ނަންބަރު 7-FINE/57/2026/17 (01 އޮކްޓޫބަރު 2026) ސިޓީއާއެކު ފޮނުއްވާފައިވާ އެ އޮފީހުގެ 2027 ވަނަ އަހަރަށް ލަފާކުރާ ބަޖެޓާއި، އޮޑިޓަރ ޖެނެރަލްގެ އޮފީހުގެ 2027 ވަނަ އަހަރަށް ކަނޑައަޅުއްވާފައިވާ "އެނުއަލް ވަރކް ޕްލޭން ފޯ 2027" (ޖަދުވަލު 1).

މި ކޮމިޓީއަށް އޮޑިޓަރ ޖެނެރަލްގެ އޮފީހުގެ 2027 ވަނަ އަހަރަށް ލަފާކުރާ ބަޖެޓު ދިރާސާކުރުމަށް ހުށަހެޅުމާ ގުޅިގެން، 12 އޮކްޓޫބަރު 2026 ގައި ބޭއްވި މި ކޮމިޓީގެ މި އަހަރުގެ 20 ވަނަ ބައްދަލުވުމުގައި އެ މައްސަލަ އެޖެންޑާކޮށް، ކޮމިޓީގެ މެންބަރުންގެ މެދުގައި މަޝްވަރާކުރިއެވެ. އަދި އޮޑިޓަރ ޖެނެރަލްގެ އޮފީހުގެ 2027 ވަނަ އަހަރަށް ލަފާކުރާ ބަޖެޓު ދިރާސާކުރުމުގެ މަސައްކަތް މި ކޮމިޓީން ކުރަމުންދިޔައިރު، އޮޑިޓަރ ޖެނެރަލްގެ އޮފީހުގެ ރިކަރަންޓް އަދި ކެޕިޓަލް ޚަރަދުތަކާ ގުޅޭގޮތުންވެސް މެންބަރުން މަޝްވަރާކުރިއެވެ. މި ބައްދަލުވުމުގައި އޮޑިޓަރ ޖެނެރަލާއި އޮޑިޓަރ ޖެނެރަލްގެ އޮފީހުގެ ކަމާގުޅުންހުރި ބޭފުޅުންނާ ބައްދަލުކޮށް އިތުރު މަޢުލޫމާތު ސާފުކޮށްފައިވެއެވެ.

Foreword

I am pleased to present the Annual Work Plan of the Auditor General's Office for 2027, the second year of implementation of our Strategic Plan 2026–2029. This plan sets out how we will use our resources over the coming year to fulfil our constitutional and legal mandate under the Audit Act and other related legislations, and to provide Parliament and the public with independent assurance on how public resources are raised, managed and used.

The plan has been prepared at a time of considerable fiscal pressure. With public debt, including guarantees, projected to exceed 126 percent of GDP and a continuing gap between government revenue and expenditure, the need for rigorous and timely oversight of public finances has never been greater. For this reason, audits of public debt, government guarantees, revenue collection, compliance with the Fiscal Responsibility Act and the whole-of-government financial statements remain at the core of our programme. We will also continue our audits of Accountable Government Agencies, local councils, State-owned enterprises, public funds and donor-funded projects, and in 2027 we will extend our work on financial sector regulators by undertaking the audit of the Capital Market Development Authority alongside the Maldives Monetary Authority.

Beyond financial and compliance assurance, this plan directs our performance, environmental, special and information systems audits towards areas of greatest risk and public interest. These include national price subsidies, inter-island transport, expatriate management, the disability allowance, the management of marine protected areas, regional waste facilities, bait fisheries management, leased tourism islands, public housing projects and high-value procurement. As government services move increasingly onto digital platforms, we will strengthen our assurance over critical data, pension, payroll and payment systems, and expand our use of full-population data analytics.

Delivering this programme depends on our people. We will continue to invest in professional certification, specialist training and knowledge exchange with our international partners, while contributing to the global auditing community through our work with INTOSAI working groups. Where new risks or priorities emerge during the year, this plan will be amended accordingly.

I extend my sincere thanks to the Public Accounts Committee of the People's Majlis for its continued support, and to the audited entities for their cooperation. We remain committed to producing audit work that adds value, strengthens accountability and makes a positive difference in the lives of the people of the Maldives.

Financial and compliance audits

Financial audits conducted by the AGO are designed to provide an independent opinion on the whole-of-government financial statements, ministries, statutory bodies, local councils, donor-funded projects and state-owned enterprises. And Compliance audits assess the extent to which audited entities comply with applicable laws, regulations and policies.

In addition to delivering the legal mandate specified in the Audit Act and the Public Finance Act, the Auditor General also carries out audits that are geared towards the audit mandate stipulated in section 30(d) of the Fiscal Responsibility Act.

Whole-of-Government Audit
3 audits

The Whole of Government Account (WGA) audit is the audit of the consolidated annual financial statements of the State, prepared by the Accountant General in accordance with the Public Finance Act. These financial statements present a consolidated view of the financial transactions of all Accountable Government Agencies and comprise the Statement of Receipts and Payments, the Statement of Comparison of Budget and Actual Amounts, and the accompanying numerical and explanatory notes. For the financial year 2026, the total State budget amounts to MVR 64.20 billion, including principal repayments, lending, and investments. Total projected revenue, grants, and financing for the year amount to MVR 66.63 billion

The WGA audit provides independent assurance on the reliability and credibility of the State's reported receipts, payments, and budget financing activities. It offers citizens, Parliament, and other key stakeholders a comprehensive "whole-of-government" perspective of the State's financial affairs, enabling a clearer understanding of how public resources are raised, managed, and utilized.

In addition, the audit promotes transparency and accountability by assisting the Legislature and citizens in holding Accountable Government Agencies responsible for the stewardship of public funds and the implementation of budgets approved by Parliament. Through the audit process, stakeholders gain confidence that public finances are reported fairly and in accordance with applicable legal and regulatory requirements.

WGA audit represents one of the most significant assurance engagements undertaken by the Auditor General's Office, providing independent oversight over the collection, allocation, and utilization of public funds across the Government of Maldives.

Revenue, Debt and Fiscal Audits
5 audits

The current estimates in the approved budget 2026 of the government show a projected revenue of MVR 40.37 billion with a total expenditure of 49.21 billion. The total public debt including guarantees is expected to increase to MVR 158.8 billion, which is more than 126% of the GDP. This significant gap between revenue and expenditure, together with the exceptionally high debt burden, increases fiscal, refinancing, liquidity and debt-servicing risks.

The audits on debt and fiscal sustainability are expected to improve the transparency and reliability of debt reporting, strengthen compliance with borrowing and approval requirements, highlight refinancing, currency, interest-rate and contingent-liability risks, and encourage prudent debt-management decisions that support long-term fiscal sustainability. Revenue audits are expected to reduce leakages, strengthen compliance enforcement and arrears management, improve internal controls, and increase the accuracy and completeness of revenue records.

Enhancing Fiscal Sustainability: Performance Audits on National Price Subsidies

National price support subsidies represent one of the most substantial recurrent expenditure burdens on the state budget, with annual allocations exceeding MVR 2.89 billion across fuel, electricity, and staple food support mechanisms. Addressing these high-outlay commitments in the 2027 Annual Work Plan (AWP) is critical to safeguarding macroeconomic stability, as untargeted price supports and international price volatility consistently drive actual outturns well beyond budgeted limits. By auditing the effectiveness, management, and fiscal sustainability of electricity, fuel, and staple food subsidies (Goal 1.3.1: Social Welfare), the AGO aims to evaluate systemic targeting inefficiencies, quantify commercial leakages, and assess import cost-efficiencies providing vital evidence to support the national transition toward means-tested cash transfers and contain escalating public spending (Goal 1.3.3: Public utility, Goal 1.3.4: Governance).

Sustaining National Transport: Performance Audit of the Raajje Transport Link

The Raajje Transport Link (RTL) ferry network is vital for decentralized socio-economic connectivity, yet it poses substantial fiscal demands with capital commitments exceeding MVR 508 million and operations requiring roughly 80% state subsidies (over MVR 488.8 million in subsidies against MVR 105.6 million in revenue).

Auditing RTL in the 2027 Annual Work Plan (AWP) will evaluate route economics, vessel procurement, and operational bottlenecks affecting long-term viability. This audit delivers direct value to citizens by identifying systemic bottlenecks to enhance scheduling and service reliability, while ensuring public funds are prudently managed to sustain affordable, equitable inter-island transport (Goal 1.3.3: Transport).

Safeguarding State Revenues and Labour Market Integrity: Expatriate Management Systems

Managing expatriate employment and fee collection is a vital regulatory function and non-tax revenue stream, yet systemic compliance gaps and undocumented labour cause substantial revenue leakages and foreign exchange outflows.

Including an audit of expatriate employment, regularization, and revenue systems in the 2027 Annual Work Plan (AWP), alongside a follow-up on the prior performance audit (Goal 1.3.5: Follow-up) will evaluate past recommendation status, quota controls, automated fee reconciliation, deposit tracking, and regularization outcomes.

This audit delivers significant value to oversight bodies by plugging fiscal leakages and enforcing institutional accountability, while protecting local labour market integrity, curbing unmonitored remittance outflows, and recovering essential public funds for national development (Goal 1.4.4: Governance).

Disability Allowance: Safeguarding Fiscal Integrity and Equitable Social Protection

Administered by NSPA and the Ministry of Social and Family Development, the disability allowance program represents a vital social safety net with substantial state budgetary allocations supporting thousands of registered persons with disabilities nationwide.

Key operational risks include administrative delays, registry completeness, accessibility hurdles in outer atolls, and the alignment of medical assessment criteria with beneficiary needs.

Auditing this program in the 2027 Annual Work Plan will evaluate registry integrity, eliminate inclusion/exclusion errors, assess disbursement timeliness, and examine support adequacy, safeguarding public funds against fraud while ensuring vulnerable citizens receive timely, dignified, and equitable support (Goal 1.3.1).

The South Ari Marine Protected Area (SAMPA), declared on 5 June 2009, is among the largest and ecologically significant protected areas in the Maldives. Renowned for its year-round aggregation of whale sharks (Fehurihi), it supports rich coral reef ecosystems, diverse marine life and several endangered species. SAMPA is a major driver of nature-based tourism, with studies estimating annual benefits over USD 9 million, making effective management critical to biodiversity conservation and sustainable economic development. The audit will assess whether SAMPA is managed efficiently and effectively to achieve its conservation objectives and deliver sustainable environmental and socio-economic outcomes.

Environmental Audit of the Regional Waste Management Center of R. Vandhoo

The establishment and operationalisation of Regional Waste Management Centres (RWMCs) is a key Government strategy for strengthening waste management. R. Vandhoo RWMC was among the first centres established and, despite over nine years of operation, continues to rely on significant Government subsidy. Sustainable and effective operation of the facility is essential to ensuring environmentally sound waste management, optimising the use of public resources, and mitigating the environmental and health impacts of improper disposal. The audit will assess whether the RWMC is operating economically and effectively in achieving its objectives, including waste processing, service delivery, resource utilisation, and compliance with national policies and standards.

Environmental Audit of the live bait fisheries in the Maldives

Livebait fisheries are critical to the Maldives' pole-and-line tuna fishery, a sector that contributes significantly to national employment, food security and export earnings. The absence of comprehensive stock assessments and long-term monitoring data further limits the authorities' ability to manage these resources effectively. Given the importance of livebait to the sustainability of the tuna fishery, the audit will assess whether the Government's governance arrangements and management measures are adequate and effective in ensuring the sustainable management of livebait fisheries in the country.

Public expenditure inherently carries risks of fraud, corruption, procurement irregularities, and the misuse of public resources, risks that undermine public trust, weaken governance, and reduce the effectiveness of government spending.

Audit quality review and monitoring

The Audit Quality Review and Monitoring Department (AQRM) is the dedicated function of the Auditor General’s Office (AGO) responsible for monitoring and improving the quality of audit work across the organisation. AQRM operates independently of the audit departments it reviews and reports on quality matters directly to the Auditor General. Its work is aligned with the revised ISSAI 140 – Quality Management for SAIs, which promotes a proactive, risk-based and continuous System of Audit Quality Management (SoAQM) rather than a traditional post-audit quality-control approach.

Mandate and objectives

AQRM provides the Auditor General with objective, independent and evidence-based assurance on the design and effectiveness of AGO’s SoAQM and the quality of individual audit engagements. Its key objectives are to:
- assess the effectiveness of AGO’s quality-management arrangements;
- promote compliance with ISSAIs, applicable legislation and AGO audit methodology;
- identify engagement-level and systemic quality deficiencies;
- conduct root-cause analysis and recommend corrective and preventive actions;
- monitor implementation of remediation measures; and
- promote a culture of professional excellence, professional scepticism and continuous improvement.

Scope and approach

AQRM covers all audit disciplines and relevant quality-management arrangements within AGO. Its work operates at two levels:

1. System-level review
Assessment of governance and leadership, risk management, ethical requirements, audit methodology, resources, information and communication, supervision and monitoring arrangements.

2. Engagement-level review
Risk-based review of individual audits through hot reviews/engagement quality reviews (EQRs) before report issuance and cold reviews of completed audit files.

Monitoring and remediation

A core responsibility of AQRM is to establish a closed-loop quality improvement process. Findings are recorded, communicated to responsible departments, assigned corrective actions and monitored until implementation. Implementation

AQRM is being introduced through a two-phase approach:

Q4 2026 Pilot
Establish the operating model, conduct 7–10 hot reviews/EQRs and 4–6 cold reviews, assess AGO’s existing quality controls against ISSAI 140, establish the findings/remediation mechanism and issue a Pilot Evaluation Report.

2027 full rollout
Implement the SoAQM across AGO, undertake mandatory EQRs for qualifying high-risk/high-judgment audits, expand cold reviews, follow up 2026 findings, conduct targeted system re-reviews and issue an Annual Quality Review Report.

Expected outcome
AQRM will strengthen the consistency, credibility and professional quality of AGO’s audit work by identifying weaknesses early, ensuring corrective actions are implemented, addressing systemic causes of deficiencies and providing the Auditor General with reliable information on the effectiveness of the Office’s System of Quality Management. This directly supports AGO’s strategic objective of delivering timely, risk-based and high-quality audits that strengthen accountability and transparency in the management of public resources.
